segments.title: Your know-how is now a product: what a skill is
talkingPoints: Why now: on November 12 Anthropic introduced Claude for Manufacturing as 17 skills, and Xero introduced Xforce, forward deployed engineers who build AI workflows around how a firm works.
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: a name, a description that says when to use it, and the steps. Claude reads the descriptions and loads the steps only when they are needed.
Committed in the project, a skill travels with the repo, so the whole team gets the same check, the same thresholds and the same PASS or FAIL language.

segments.title: Build 1: the analyst's check becomes data-quality-gate
talkingPoints: In a sandbox folder, Claude Code generates a fictional orders file with four planted problems. Sample data only, so we know the right answer before Claude does.
The description names the trigger in the words an analyst uses; the body is her routine: freshness, duplicate keys, required fields, unreasonable amounts.
Test it the honest way: ask in plain words, without naming the skill, and watch which skill loads.
segments.onScreenBuild: Claude Code runs instruction 1: creates morning-check, the SAMPLE DATA orders file with four planted problems and the data-quality-gate skill; Ali asks in plain words and the report finds all four and says BLOCK.
segments.chatPrompt: Type READY when your own skills folder exists, or STUCK and a mentor will jump in.

segments.title: The mistake: a skill that never fires
talkingPoints: On a throwaway copy, keep the same steps and change only the description to 'Helps with data.' Ask the same plain question.
Direct invocation proves the steps run; a plain-words question tests whether Claude can tell when the skill applies. A vague description names no trigger and no output.
Delete the copy: with real skills beside it, the vague one loses. One sentence is the difference between a check that runs and one nobody can find.
segments.onScreenBuild: Claude Code runs instruction 2: makes the data-helper copy with the vague description, reports whether it loaded on the plain question, then deletes it; data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary stay.
segments.chatPrompt: Diagnostic: it works when you type the slash command but not when you ask in plain words. What do you inspect first?
segments.visual: Two descriptions side by side, 'Helps with data.' crossed out in red, the trigger-naming description in green beneath it.

talkingPoints: The gate stopped the bad number from publishing. The CFO still needs to know what happened, what it means and who owns it.

Detect, then communicate: two skills, one workflow. Diagnosis (etl-failure-triage) is the third, and it is your build-along.

soundBites.text: Anthropic just shipped manufacturing know-how as 17 skills; your own routine judgment is next, not last.
79% of manufacturers still enter data by hand, and every manual check you run is a skill waiting to be written.
The biggest mistake you can make is a vague description; 'helps with data' never fires, not once.
Detect, diagnose, communicate: every incident needs all three, and a skill can run each one for you.
Within a year, your team's best checks will live in skills, not in one person's memory.
You don't need a better prompt; you need one Claude remembers and runs the same way every time.
The analyst is out today, so the check you never wrote down did not run, and revenue looked down 18%.
soundBites.story: This is an illustrative scenario from our curriculum. It is 8:05 AM. The executive dashboard says revenue is down 18%. The overnight job says SUCCESS: it ran clean, on schedule, no errors. But the analyst who checks those numbers by hand every morning is out today, and nobody else knows her check. The data has a duplicate order, a missing region and a negative amount. A green job only proves it ran. Her check should not live in her head.

soundBites.text: A skill is only a folder: a name, a description that says when, and the steps you would never skip.
Xero is pairing accounting firms with forward deployed engineers, and you already know the one thing they must learn: how your firm works.
Never test a new skill on live company data; a sample file fails safely and costs you nothing.
We built a skill in ten minutes that catches four problems a green pipeline never flagged.
A green pipeline only proves the job ran; it never proved the data was right.

slides.title: Build 1: data-quality-gate
bullets: Ask in plain words, watch which skill loads
slides.visual: Claude Code on the left running the instruction, the generated SKILL.md on the right.
slides.instruction:
Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste.
1. Open the morning-check folder (it already holds two prepared skills, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary) and create a sample-data folder inside it.
   # WHY: a sandbox. Nothing in this folder touches a real company system.
2. Generate a fictional orders file for a made-up retailer, about 40 rows: order id, region, revenue amount, load timestamp. Put SAMPLE DATA as the first line. Plant exactly four problems: one duplicate order id, one missing region, one negative revenue amount, and a load timestamp older than 48 hours.
   # WHY: these are the four problems the analyst catches by hand. Planting them means we know the right answer before Claude does.
3. Create a project skill named data-quality-gate in this folder. Description: "Use when the user asks to validate a dataset, CSV, ETL output, query result, or dashboard source before publication." Steps: check freshness, duplicate keys, required fields and unreasonable amounts; give each check PASS, WARN or FAIL with the row that proves it; end with PUBLISH or BLOCK.
   # WHY: the description says when, the steps say how. This is the analyst's morning routine, written down once.
4. Tell me when it is ready and stop. I will ask, in my own words and without naming the skill, whether the orders file is safe to publish.
   # WHY: asking in plain words tests whether the description does its job.
Stop when the report finds all four planted problems and says BLOCK.
slides.speakerNote: Narrate the decisions, not the characters: why sample data, why four planted problems, why the description is written in an analyst's words. Then ask: is this orders file safe to publish to the revenue dashboard?
slides.publicValue: Main build footage: a first Claude skill in a sandbox folder

slides.title: The gate decides before anyone sees it
bullets: PASS, WARN or FAIL per check
slides.visual: The gate flowchart full screen, BLOCK in red.
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR
  F[Orders file] --> G[Four checks]
  G --> H[Pass Warn Fail]
  H --> I{Safe?}
  I --> P[PUBLISH]
  I --> X[BLOCK]
slides.speakerNote: Point at the evidence column: every FAIL names the row. A check that cannot show its evidence is an opinion. Ask the room to type READY or STUCK before moving on.
slides.publicValue: Teaching clip: how a data check decides publish or block

slides.title: Break it: 'Helps with data.'
slides.visual: Split screen: the data-helper SKILL.md with the one-line description, beside Claude's answer showing which skill it used.
slides.instruction:
Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste.
1. Make a throwaway copy of data-quality-gate called data-helper with the same steps, but set its description to "Helps with data." Leave data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary in the skills folder.
   # WHY: same steps, vague description. Only the trigger changes, so whatever happens next is the description's doing.
2. Tell me when it is ready and stop. I will ask the same plain question about the orders file.
   # WHY: typing the slash command would prove the steps run. A plain question tests whether Claude can tell when this skill applies.
3. After my question, report which skill loaded, and what in data-helper's description helped or failed to help it compete.
4. Delete data-helper and list the skills that remain.
Stop when data-helper is gone and data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary remain.
slides.speakerNote: This is the deliberate failure: data-helper competes with data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary, so 'Helps with data' should lose. If it fires anyway, say so out loud and compare the two descriptions. Confirm the copy is deleted before moving on.
slides.publicValue: High-retention teardown: the description mistake and its fix

slides.title: Slash works. Plain words do not. Why?
slides.visual: Three large option tiles plus 'CSV filename'; the vote bars fill as answers arrive.
slides.speakerNote: Expect most of the room on the description, and a few on body length. Reveal: the slash command proves the steps can run; a plain question tests whether the description helps Claude recognize when the skill applies.
slides.publicValue: Interaction clip: why a skill does not trigger

slides.title: Build 2: executive-dashboard-brief
bullets: A second skill for a different reader
slides.visual: Claude Code's finished executive brief on the left, the list of both skills with their descriptions on the right.
slides.instruction:
Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste.
1. Create a second project skill named executive-dashboard-brief. Description: "Use when a data-quality or incident report must be turned into an update for executives or leadership." Steps: write status, business impact, evidence, decision needed, owner and next update time, in under 150 words, with no SQL and no log lines.
   # WHY: the technical report is right but written for the wrong reader. Leadership needs a decision, not a data dump.
2. Run data-quality-gate on the orders file again, then hand its report to executive-dashboard-brief.
   # WHY: detect, then communicate. Two skills, one workflow, and neither one lives in a person's head.
3. Show me the brief, then list every skill in the folder with its description.
   # WHY: the list is what your teammates will see. If a description is unclear here, it will be unclear to Claude too.
Stop when the brief names the BLOCK decision, an owner and a next-update time in under 150 words.
slides.speakerNote: Read the brief aloud as if you were the CFO. Ask the room: could you act on this? Then point out that diagnosis, the middle step, is the build-along.
slides.publicValue: Payoff footage: two skills turn an incident into a decision

questions.q: Where are you watching from, and what kind of check do you run by hand at work?
questions.answer: No right answer. Read three out loud and keep them for the hot seat.

questions.q: The ETL run is green, but the dashboard looks wrong. What should happen first?
options: Validate the output against its data-quality contract
Ask leadership which number looks suspicious
questions.answer: Validate the output against its data-quality contract. A green pipeline proves the job ran; it does not prove the data is trustworthy.

questions.q: Which part helps Claude recognize when a skill is relevant?
questions.answer: Description. Claude scans the descriptions to decide when to load a skill; the description is the routing logic, not documentation.

questions.q: The skill works when you type /data-quality-gate, but not when you ask 'Is this dataset safe to publish?' What do you inspect first?
questions.answer: Skill description. Direct invocation proves the steps run; a plain-words question tests whether the description helps Claude recognize when the skill applies.

questions.q: What belongs in the executive update?
options: Status, impact, evidence, decision, owner and next update
A general note that IT is investigating
questions.answer: Status, impact, evidence, decision, owner and next update. Leadership needs a decision product, not a technical data dump.

questions.q: Name one check that would stop running if you were out tomorrow. How ready is it to become a skill?
options: I have not thought of one yet
I know the check but not the words
I could write its description now
questions.answer: A good answer names a specific check, the words a colleague would use to ask for it, and the one thing it must never do (for example, send anything without a person approving).

questions.q: What does allowed-tools in a skill do?
options: Permanently restricts the skill to those tools
Pre-approves the named tools for the turn that invokes the skill
questions.answer: Pre-approves the named tools for the turn that invokes the skill. It does not restrict which tools are available; permission settings still govern the rest.

questions.q: From 'I watched' to 'I could build this tonight', where are you?
options: I could build it with the three instructions
I could build it from memory
questions.answer: Any honest answer is right. 'With the three instructions' is this week's target; 'I watched' means start the build-along with instruction 1 tonight.

demo.goal: In a sandbox folder that holds two prepared skills (etl-failure-triage and csv-summary), turn the analyst's morning check into a data-quality-gate skill on a fictional orders file, break it with a vague description and restore it, then add executive-dashboard-brief so one plain-words question ends in a decision leadership can act on.
steps: Before the show: create etl-failure-triage and csv-summary in the morning-check folder's skills (prepared, not built live; csv-summary describes a CSV's columns and row counts), so the teardown has real competition.
Cold open: show the finished BLOCK report from the prepared folder (recorded run ready in tab 2).
Build 1: Claude Code creates morning-check, the SAMPLE DATA orders file with four planted problems and data-quality-gate; Ali asks in plain words whether the file is safe to publish.

Teardown: a throwaway data-helper copy with the description 'Helps with data.'; ask the same question, report which skill loaded (data-helper competes with data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary), then delete it.
Build 2: Claude Code creates executive-dashboard-brief, runs the gate again and hands its report to the brief.
Close the loop: list every skill with its description and confirm data-helper is gone.
claudeCodeInstructions: Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste. In the morning-check folder (it already holds two prepared skills, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary), create a sample-data folder, generate a fictional retailer orders file with SAMPLE DATA on the first line and exactly four planted problems (a duplicate order id, a missing region, a negative revenue amount, a load timestamp older than 48 hours), and create a project skill named data-quality-gate with the description 'Use when the user asks to validate a dataset, CSV, ETL output, query result, or dashboard source before publication.' and steps that give PASS, WARN or FAIL per check with evidence and end with PUBLISH or BLOCK. Then stop and wait for my question.

Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste. Make a throwaway copy of data-quality-gate called data-helper whose description is only 'Helps with data.', leave data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary where they are, and wait for my question. After it, report which skill loaded and why data-helper did or did not, then delete data-helper and list the skills that remain.

Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste. Create a project skill named executive-dashboard-brief with the description 'Use when a data-quality or incident report must be turned into an update for executives or leadership.' that writes status, impact, evidence, decision, owner and next update in under 150 words, run data-quality-gate on the orders file, hand its report to the brief, show the brief and list every skill with its description.
whatCouldGoWrong: The vague 'Helps with data.' skill fires anyway even with data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary beside it: say so, read the two descriptions side by side, and explain that a team folder with twenty skills makes the collision worse, not better.
Claude Code does not pick up a new skill until a new message or session: ask it to confirm the skill is listed before asking the question.
The generated sample data has five problems or three, not four: ask Claude Code to list the planted problems before the build, and regenerate if the count is wrong.
The generated data uses a real company name: regenerate with obviously fictional names before going live.
The brief runs long or includes log lines: point at the 150-word rule in the description and have Claude Code tighten the skill, which is itself the lesson.
demo.fallback: Tab 2 holds a recorded run of all three instructions against the same sample data, a saved copy of the finished morning-check folder, and screenshots of the BLOCK report and the executive brief. If any build stalls past two minutes, switch to the recording and narrate it.

students.buildAlong: Rebuild tonight's workflow on a sample file you generate, never real data: data-quality-gate, executive-dashboard-brief, and etl-failure-triage, which sat prepared in tonight's folder but was not built live; it reads the run's log and ranks the likely causes with evidence. Prove each skill fires from a plain-words question, not the slash command, and commit all three to .claude/skills/.
students.applyToOwnPlan: Your generated build plan arrives in Week 3. Before then, write down the one check from your own job that would stop running if you were out tomorrow, and draft its description in the words a colleague would use to ask for it. Bring it to the next session; it becomes the first skill in your own plan.

coldOpen.title: The finished check: BLOCK, with four reasons
coldOpen.body: A sample orders file nobody has checked. One plain question: is it safe to publish? Claude loads the skill you are about to build, finds four problems with the row that proves each, and says BLOCK before the dashboard ever sees it.

teach.title: Know-how is shipping as skills
teach.body: On November 12 Anthropic introduced Claude for Manufacturing as 17 skills, each built to end with a person's review. The same day Xero introduced Xforce, which pairs accounting firms with forward deployed engineers who build AI workflows around how each firm works.
bullets: Nov 12: Xforce by Xero, forward deployed engineers
Every manufacturing skill ends with a person's review
teach.script:
SITUATION: The cold open just showed the finished check; now the room needs the reason it matters this month.
ROOM: Both announcement pages open in tabs, ready to switch to.
MOOD: Matter-of-fact, a little urgent.
OPEN: Two companies said the same thing on the same day.
DO: Switch to each source page for five seconds so the room sees it is real.
NOTE: Re-check both pages on the air date before trusting the slide.
SAY: Anthropic shipped manufacturing know-how as 17 skills. Xero is sending engineers into accounting firms to build workflows around how they work.
SAY: Your routine judgment is what gets packaged next. Tonight you learn to package it yourself.

teach.title: What a skill is
teach.body: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md: a name, a description that says when to use it, and the steps. Claude reads every description first and loads a skill's steps only when one matches, so the description decides whether your skill is ever used.
bullets: The steps load only when needed
teach.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Your question] --> B[Scans descriptions]
  B --> C[Matching skill]
  C --> D[Steps load]
  D --> E[Same answer]
teach.script:
SITUATION: The why is landed; now the what, before anyone builds.
ROOM: The flowchart, ready to full-screen.
MOOD: Calm teacher; this is the one concept everything hangs on.
OPEN: Here is how Claude decides to use something you taught it.
DO: Click the diagram to full screen and point at each box.
NOTE: Spend most of the time on the second box; the rest of the night depends on it.
SAY: You ask a question. Claude scans the descriptions. If one matches, it opens that skill and follows the steps.
SAY: That is why the description is the most important sentence you will write tonight.

teach.title: Build 1: data-quality-gate
teach.body: In a sandbox folder, Claude Code generates a fictional orders file with four planted problems and writes the analyst's routine as a skill. Then we ask in plain words, without naming it, and watch which skill loads.

code.label: Build data-quality-gate
code.code:
Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste.
1. Open the morning-check folder (it already holds two prepared skills, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary) and create a sample-data folder inside it.
   # WHY: a sandbox. Nothing in this folder touches a real company system.
2. Generate a fictional orders file for a made-up retailer, about 40 rows: order id, region, revenue amount, load timestamp. Put SAMPLE DATA as the first line. Plant exactly four problems: one duplicate order id, one missing region, one negative revenue amount, and a load timestamp older than 48 hours.
   # WHY: these are the four problems the analyst catches by hand. Planting them means we know the right answer before Claude does.
3. Create a project skill named data-quality-gate in this folder. Description: "Use when the user asks to validate a dataset, CSV, ETL output, query result, or dashboard source before publication." Steps: check freshness, duplicate keys, required fields and unreasonable amounts; give each check PASS, WARN or FAIL with the row that proves it; end with PUBLISH or BLOCK.
   # WHY: the description says when, the steps say how.
4. Tell me when it is ready and stop. I will ask, in my own words and without naming the skill, whether the orders file is safe to publish.
Stop when the report finds all four planted problems and says BLOCK.
code.expectedResult: A morning-check folder with a SAMPLE DATA orders file and a data-quality-gate skill; a plain-words question returns four FAIL/WARN rows with evidence and BLOCK.
code.stopCondition: The report finds all four planted problems and says BLOCK.
code.rescue: If the skill does not load, ask Claude Code to list the skills it can see and confirm data-quality-gate is there before asking again.

teach.script:
SITUATION: First build of the night; the room has just seen what a skill is.
ROOM: Claude Code open on the sandbox folder (two prepared skills in it); tab 2 has the recorded run.
MOOD: Hands-on, unhurried.
OPEN: Let's write the analyst's check down, once.
DO: Paste the instruction and narrate why each step exists while it runs.
NOTE: If it stalls past two minutes, switch to tab 2 and narrate the recording.
SAY: Notice the description is written in the words an analyst uses, not the words an engineer uses.
SAY: Now I will ask the way a colleague would: is this orders file safe to publish to the revenue dashboard?

teach.title: The gate decides before anyone sees it
teach.body: Every check returns PASS, WARN or FAIL with the row that proves it, and the skill ends with one recommendation: PUBLISH or BLOCK. A check that cannot show its evidence is an opinion.
bullets: PASS, WARN or FAIL per check
teach.diagram:
flowchart LR
  F[Orders file] --> G[Four checks]
  G --> H[Pass Warn Fail]
  H --> I{Safe?}
  I --> P[PUBLISH]
  I --> X[BLOCK]
teach.script:
SITUATION: The report just came back BLOCK; now explain why its shape matters.
ROOM: The report on the right of the screen, the flowchart ready.
MOOD: Satisfied, then serious.
OPEN: Look at the column on the right of that report.
DO: Ask the room to type READY or STUCK before moving on.
NOTE: Send mentors to anyone who types STUCK before the teardown starts.
SAY: Every FAIL names the row that proves it. That is what makes this a control and not a hunch.
SAY: And it ends in one decision a person can act on: publish or block.

teach.title: Break it: 'Helps with data.'
teach.body: Same steps, one change: the description becomes 'Helps with data.' It names no trigger and no output, so Claude has nothing to match a plain question against. With real skills beside it, the vague one loses. Then we delete the copy.

code.label: The vague description
code.code:
Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste.
1. Make a throwaway copy of data-quality-gate called data-helper with the same steps, but set its description to "Helps with data." Leave data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary in the skills folder.
   # WHY: only the trigger changes, so whatever happens next is the description's doing.
2. Tell me when it is ready and stop. I will ask the same plain question about the orders file.
   # WHY: a slash command proves the steps run; a plain question tests whether Claude can tell when this skill applies.
3. After my question, report which skill loaded, and what in data-helper's description helped or failed to help it compete.
4. Delete data-helper and list the skills that remain.
Stop when data-helper is gone and data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary remain.
code.expectedResult: Claude reports that data-quality-gate, not data-helper, loaded and why; data-helper is deleted.
code.stopCondition: data-helper is gone; data-quality-gate, etl-failure-triage and csv-summary remain.
code.rescue: If the vague skill fires anyway, say so: name the competitors it beat and why that was luck, then read the two descriptions side by side.

teach.script:
SITUATION: The skill works; now the mistake almost everyone makes first.
ROOM: The working skill in place; the poll slide comes next.
MOOD: Playful, then pointed.
OPEN: Let's write the description most people write on their first try.
DO: Run the instruction, ask the plain question, then read Claude's explanation aloud.
NOTE: Confirm out loud that data-helper is deleted before Build 2.
SAY: Same steps. One line changed. That line is the only way Claude knows when to use what you taught it.
SAY: Helps with data names no trigger and no output. A team folder full of those is a folder nobody can use.

teach.title: Build 2: executive-dashboard-brief
teach.body: The gate stopped the bad number. Leadership still needs status, impact, evidence, decision, owner and next update. A second skill turns the technical report into that, in under 150 words.

code.label: Build the executive brief
code.code:
Run these steps yourself — do not print commands for me to copy and paste.
1. Create a second project skill named executive-dashboard-brief. Description: "Use when a data-quality or incident report must be turned into an update for executives or leadership." Steps: write status, business impact, evidence, decision needed, owner and next update time, in under 150 words, with no SQL and no log lines.
   # WHY: the technical report is right but written for the wrong reader.
2. Run data-quality-gate on the orders file again, then hand its report to executive-dashboard-brief.
   # WHY: detect, then communicate. Two skills, one workflow.
3. Show me the brief, then list every skill in the folder with its description.
   # WHY: the list is what your teammates will see.
Stop when the brief names the BLOCK decision, an owner and a next-update time in under 150 words.
code.expectedResult: A brief of under 150 words naming status BLOCKED, impact, owner and next update; two skills listed with their descriptions.
code.stopCondition: The brief names the BLOCK decision, an owner and a next-update time.
code.rescue: If the brief runs long or quotes log lines, have Claude Code tighten the skill's steps and run it again.

teach.script:
SITUATION: The failure is fixed; the incident is not over, because leadership is waiting.
ROOM: The restored gate; the CFO story beat just played.
MOOD: Purposeful, a recovery.
OPEN: The data team has the answer. The CFO still does not.
DO: Run the instruction, then read the finished brief aloud as if you were the CFO.
NOTE: Ask the room whether they could act on it before moving on.
SAY: Two skills, one workflow. Detect, then communicate.
SAY: The middle step, diagnosis, is the one you build this week.

teach.title: Detect, diagnose, communicate
teach.body: Detection protects the business. Diagnosis restores the system. Communication closes the loop. Tonight we built the first and the last; the middle one is your build-along.
teach.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Detect] --> B[Diagnose]
  B --> C[Communicate]
  C --> D[Decision]
teach.script:
SITUATION: Both builds are done; give the room the pattern to take home.
ROOM: The three-step flowchart, Diagnose outlined.
MOOD: Summing up, confident.
OPEN: Every incident needs three things.
DO: Point at Diagnose and leave it there while you speak.
NOTE: This sets up the build-along, so name it clearly.
SAY: Detection is for the business, diagnosis is for the engineers, communication is for leadership.
SAY: We built the first and the last tonight. The middle one is yours.

interactions.q: Where are you watching from, and what kind of check do you run by hand at work?
interactions.reveal: No right answer. Keep these for the hot seat.
interactions.title: What do you check by hand?

interactions.q: The ETL run is green, but the dashboard looks wrong. What should happen first?
options: Validate the output against its data-quality contract
Ask leadership which number looks suspicious
interactions.reveal: A green pipeline proves that the job ran. It does not prove that the resulting data is trustworthy.
interactions.title: Green job, wrong number
interactions.presenterTip: Expect the room to split between validate and rerun.

interactions.q: Which part helps Claude recognize when a skill is relevant?
interactions.reveal: Claude scans the descriptions to decide when to load a skill. The description is the routing logic.
interactions.title: What makes a skill fire?
interactions.presenterTip: Ask before Build 1 runs; the build proves the answer.

interactions.q: The skill works when you type /data-quality-gate, but not when you ask 'Is this dataset safe to publish?' What do you inspect first?
interactions.reveal: Direct invocation proves the steps run. A plain question tests whether the description helps Claude recognize when the skill applies.
interactions.title: Slash works. Plain words do not.
interactions.presenterTip: Reveal right after the vague skill is tested.

interactions.q: What belongs in the executive update?
options: Status, impact, evidence, decision, owner and next update
A general note that IT is investigating
interactions.reveal: Leadership needs a decision product, not a technical data dump.
interactions.title: What goes in the brief?
interactions.presenterTip: Take responses, reveal, then go straight into Build 2.

interactions.q: Name one check that would stop running if you were out tomorrow. How ready is it to become a skill?
options: I have not thought of one yet
I know the check but not the words
I could write its description now
interactions.reveal: A good answer names a specific check, the words a colleague would use to ask for it, and the one thing it must never do.
interactions.title: Your check
interactions.presenterTip: Pick hot-seat volunteers from the last two options.

interactions.q: What does allowed-tools in a skill do?
options: Permanently restricts the skill to those tools
Pre-approves the named tools for the turn that invokes the skill
interactions.reveal: Pre-approval and restriction are different controls. allowed-tools pre-approves tools for the turn; permission settings govern the rest.
interactions.title: Tool permissions, precisely
interactions.presenterTip: Expendable if time is short; read the reveal exactly as written.

interactions.q: From 'I watched' to 'I could build this tonight', where are you?
options: I could build it with the three instructions
I could build it from memory
interactions.reveal: Any honest answer is right. 'With the three instructions' is this week's target.
interactions.title: Where are you?
interactions.presenterTip: Ask for honest answers; no right one.

storyBeats.title: The analyst who catches this is out today.
storyBeats.body: The dashboard says revenue is down 18%. The overnight job says SUCCESS. The analyst who checks those numbers by hand every morning is out, and nobody else knows her check.
storyBeats.punch: She should not be the control. The check should.

storyBeats.title: A steel shipment slips two weeks.
storyBeats.body: In Anthropic's Claude for Manufacturing example, Claude finds the affected customer orders and the steel stock at other sites. It can release a purchase order to another supplier, but only after the buyer approves.
storyBeats.punch: The know-how is packaged. The decision stays hers.

storyBeats.title: The data team has an answer. The CFO is still waiting.
storyBeats.body: The report is correct and full of row numbers and timestamps. The CFO has a board call in an hour and needs impact, a decision, an owner and the next update.
storyBeats.punch: A technically correct answer can still be the wrong communication product.
